title: Micah’s graven/molten image vowed to Jehovah—relative cult still called a most grave crime
source_text: XXX. Ejusdem quoque criminis reus fuit Micha ille & Mater ejus, de quibus narratur historia quaedam in libro Judicum capite decimo septimo. Nempe quum ille matri suae furatus esset mille & centum argenteos, & illa super eo perplexa & anxia esset, ultro tandem fassus est penes se esse istam pecuniam, & eam matri suae restituit. Illa vero dixit se consecravisse & vovisse hoc argentum Domino, seu Jehovae, ut habet textus Hebraicus. Atque ex ea pecuniae summa tulit ducentos argenteos, & dedit eos argentario, ut faceret ex eis sculptile atque conflatile, quod fuit in Domo Michae. Qui aediculam quoque in ea Deo separavit, & consecravit unum filiorum suorum, qui factus est ei Sacerdos. Cumque postea filio substituisset Levitam, qui in ista aedicula, Sacerdotio fungeretur, dixit se in posterum sperare quod Jehovah benefaceret ipsi, habenti Levitici generis Sacerdotem. Ex quibus patet sculptile & conflatile istud, ex eorum mente, fuisse vero Deo, nempe, Jehovae consecratum, & eos cultum istum retulisse ad Jehovam, a quo remunerationem illius expectabant. Unde clare sequitur, adorationem ab illis imagini exhibitam non fuisse nisi relativam, quae tamen ut scelus gravissimum in scriptura reprehenditur.
pass_a_gloss: Of the same crime also that Micah and his Mother were guilty, of whom a certain history is narrated in the book of Judges chapter seventeen. Namely when he had stolen from his mother a thousand and a hundred silver pieces, and she was perplexed and anxious over it, at length he freely confessed that that money was with him, and restored it to his mother. But she said that she had consecrated and vowed this silver to the Lord, or Jehovah, as the Hebrew text has. And from that sum of money she took two hundred silver pieces, and gave them to a silversmith, that he might make from them a graven and a molten thing, which was in the House of Micah. Who also separated a little shrine in it for God, and consecrated one of his sons, who became a Priest to him. And when afterward he had substituted a Levite for his son, to discharge the Priesthood in that little shrine, he said that he hoped thereafter that Jehovah would do him good, having a Priest of the Levitical kind. From which it is plain that that graven and molten thing, from their mind, had been consecrated to the true God, namely Jehovah, and that they referred that cult to Jehovah, from whom they expected the remuneration of it. Whence it clearly follows that the adoration exhibited by them to the image was nothing but relative, which yet is reprehended in Scripture as a most grave crime.
pass_b_english: Micah’s household shrine: silver vowed to Jehovah, Levite priest, hope of Jehovah’s blessing.
The cult is textbook relative—and Scripture still brands it a most grave crime.
